full_judgment:
Nozrul Islam Chowdhury, J: This Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, was issued at the instance of the preemptees as petitioners, calling upon the pre-emptor opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 21-5-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Additional Court, Narayanganj in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 21 of 1999 affirming those dated 11-3-1999 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Rupganj, Narayanganj in Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1996 allowing pre-emption under, section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court many deem fit and proper. 

 2. Short facts, necessary for the purpose of the Rule is that the opposite Party Nos. 1-4 as pre-ernptors instituted Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1996 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 before the Senior Assistant Judge, Rupganj, Narayanganj for pre-emption of .04½ acres of land in Plot No.653 appertaining to SA Khatian No.140 of Mouja Vulta under police station-Rupganj within the district of Narayanganj. 

 3. The case of the pre-emptor, in brief, is that the pre-emptors .are co-sharers by, inheritance in the case holding and that the opposite party No.4 without serving any notice under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 upon the pre-emptors, sold the case land in favour of the pre-emptees by a registered kabala dated 11-2-1996 and the purchasers are strangers in the, holdings. The pre-emptors having come to know about a deed on 15-4-1996, obtained the' certified copy of the impugned kabala on 16-4-1996 and thereafter, filed the pre-emption case on 27-5-1996 seeking pre- emption of the case land as. aforesaid. 

 (2) judgments of other Courts shall contain a concise statement of the case, the points for determination, the decision thereon, and the reasons for such decision." 

 18. Under the circumstances, as stated above, it further appears that though this court is dealing with a judgment of affirmance based on concurrent finding of facts yet those findings being devoid of any reasoning, derived upon assessment of evidence on record, those are not at all binding upon this court, since the said findings cannot but be termed as perverse as has been indicated above. In this connection relying upon the full bench decision as referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, I find that the provisions of sub-rule 2 of rule 4 of Order XX is a guideline, mandatory for both the trial Court as well as the appellate Court and that being so, the trial Court as well as the appellate Court should apply their mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the issues involved therein and upon assessment of evidence on record, should give a reasoned judgment thereon not only to satisfy their own conscience but also of the litigants allowing them to understand that all their evidence has been evaluated and their contentions and arguments duly considered by the court concerned. This is of vital importance, more particularly when confidence of the litigant in courts is built upon the quality of judgments it delivers.
